title: What a Kayo Pattern Is
description: A kayo pattern — the term used throughout this database — is a repeating motif in data or design that creates ambiguity, and whose resolution 'knocks out' the ambiguity the way a knockout ends a bout. A delimiter that also appears inside fields, a date like 03/04/05 readable three ways, a name stored surname-first in one system and given-first in another: each is a kayo pattern. The database catalogs these patterns by family and gives each a deterministic resolution rule, so the same ambiguity is knocked out the same way every time.
demo:
print('kayo pattern = repeating ambiguity motif + deterministic resolution rule')
print('resolve once, knock it out everywhere: same input -> same resolution')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Delimiter Collision
description: Delimiter collision is the kayo pattern where the separator character also appears inside field values — commas inside CSV addresses, pipes inside piped logs. The resolution rule is quoting with an escape convention (RFC 4180: wrap fields in double quotes, double any inner quote), or switching to a delimiter proven absent by a pre-scan. Resolvers must handle the pattern, not the instance: parse by state machine, never by naive split.
demo:
import csv, io
row = '"Doe, John",42,"New York, NY"'
print('naive split:', row.split(','))
print('resolved:', next(csv.reader(io.StringIO(row))))
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Homograph Collision
description: Homograph collision is the kayo pattern where two different entities share one written form — 'Springfield' the city versus thirty other Springfields, 'Apple' the fruit versus the company. The resolution rule is contextual disambiguation: attach a namespace, authority code, or coordinate to each mention at ingest, and never merge records on bare strings. Search systems resolve it with entity linking against a knowledge base.
demo:
print('Springfield x34 in the US: attach state/county/coordinates at ingest')
print('rule: never merge records on bare strings; link to an authority')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Unit Ambiguity
description: Unit ambiguity is the kayo pattern where a bare number hides its unit — is '12' inches or centimeters, pounds or kilos? The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter loss (pound-seconds vs newton-seconds) is the famous casualty. The resolution rule is that every quantity is stored as value-plus-unit and converted through a single unit registry; bare numbers are rejected at the boundary.
demo:
print('Mars Climate Orbiter (1999): lb-s vs N-s -> $125M lesson')
print('rule: store value+unit; convert via one registry; reject bare numbers')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Date-Format Ambiguity
description: Date-format ambiguity is the kayo pattern where 03/04/05 means March 4 or April 3, 2005 or 1905, depending on locale. The resolution rule is ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) for all storage and interchange, with locale-specific formats confined to display. Ingest resolvers try explicit format lists in documented priority order and flag anything still ambiguous for human review rather than guessing.
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Name-Order Ambiguity
description: Name-order ambiguity is the kayo pattern where 'Li Wei' or 'Garcia Maria' may be family-name-first or given-name-first depending on culture. The resolution rule is to store family name and given name in separate fields with an explicit order flag, and to display per locale convention. Merging systems that concatenate names into one field manufactures this pattern; splitting it at the source knocks it out.
demo:
print('store: family_name + given_name + order_flag (separate fields)')
print('display per locale; never concatenate-then-guess')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Duplicate-Key Drift
description: Duplicate-key drift is the kayo pattern where supposedly unique identifiers repeat — customer IDs reused after deletion, SKUs duplicated across regions. The resolution rule is surrogate keys (system-generated, never reused) for identity, with business codes treated as attributes that may collide. A drift detector counts key frequencies on every load and quarantines collisions before they merge.
demo:
keys = ['A1','A2','A1','B1']
from collections import Counter
print('drift scan:', dict(Counter(keys)))
print('rule: surrogate keys for identity; business codes are attributes')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Encoding Drift
description: Encoding drift is the kayo pattern where text decoded in the wrong encoding produces mojibake — 'café' becoming 'cafÃ©' when UTF-8 bytes are read as Latin-1. The resolution rule is UTF-8 everywhere with BOM detection at ingest, plus a repair pass that recognizes the classic double-encoding signatures. The pattern repeats wherever legacy systems meet modern ones.
demo:
bad = 'cafÃ©'
print('mojibake:', bad, '-> repaired:', bad.encode('latin-1').decode('utf-8'))
print('rule: UTF-8 everywhere; detect BOM; repair double-encoding signatures')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Truncation Ambiguity
description: Truncation ambiguity is the kayo pattern where shortened values collide — 10-character product codes cut to 8, names abbreviated past uniqueness. The resolution rule is to truncate only for display while storing the full value, and to verify that any truncated key remains unique before it is used as one. Silent truncation in ETL pipelines is the usual manufacturer of this pattern.
demo:
vals = ['WIDGET-1001-A', 'WIDGET-1001-B']
print('truncated to 12 chars:', [v[:12] for v in vals], '-> COLLISION')
print('rule: truncate for display only; store full; verify uniqueness')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Case-Fold Collision
description: Case-fold collision is the kayo pattern where 'Smith', 'SMITH', and 'smith' are one person to a human but three keys to a database. The resolution rule is canonical case-folding (Unicode casefold, not just lower()) at match time while preserving original casing for display. Turkish dotted-I and German ß are the classic traps that naive lowercasing misses.
demo:
print('SMITH'.casefold() == 'smith'.casefold(), '(use casefold, not lower)')
print('preserve original casing for display; fold only for matching')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Leading-Zero Loss
description: Leading-zero loss is the kayo pattern where '00742' becomes 742 when a spreadsheet or parser coerces a code to a number — destroying ZIP codes, part numbers, and IDs. The resolution rule is to type all identifiers as text from the first keystroke, and to validate with a pattern (regex) rather than a numeric range. Once the zeros are gone they cannot be recovered by guessing.
demo:
print('"00742" as number ->', int('00742'), '(zeros destroyed)')
print('rule: identifiers are TEXT from the first keystroke; validate by pattern')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Currency-Symbol Ambiguity
description: Currency-symbol ambiguity is the kayo pattern where '$' means USD, CAD, AUD, MXN, and a dozen others, and '¥' means JPY or CNY. The resolution rule is ISO 4217 codes (USD, EUR, JPY) on every monetary value, with symbols confined to localized display. Financial merges that sum across bare '$' amounts manufacture phantom totals.
demo:
print('$ -> USD? CAD? AUD? MXN? | rule: ISO 4217 codes (USD, EUR, JPY)')
print('symbols for display only; never sum across bare symbols')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Timezone Ambiguity
description: Timezone ambiguity is the kayo pattern where '3:00 PM' or a bare timestamp hides its zone — and daylight-saving transitions make some local times occur twice or never. The resolution rule is UTC for storage with the original zone recorded separately, and ISO 8601 offsets for interchange. Scheduling systems resolve it by converting at display time, never at rest.
demo:
print('store UTC + original zone; interchange with ISO 8601 offsets')
print('DST trap: some local times occur twice or never — convert at display')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Null-vs-Empty Confusion
description: Null-vs-empty confusion is the kayo pattern where missing data (NULL: never provided) and empty data ('': provided but blank) are treated as the same — corrupting 'declined to answer' into 'answered nothing.' The resolution rule is a three-state model (unknown / empty / value) with explicit sentinels, and queries that distinguish IS NULL from = ''. The distinction matters most in medical, survey, and compliance data.
demo:
print('three states: NULL (never provided) vs empty (provided blank) vs value')
print('rule: IS NULL is not = \'\'; model all three explicitly')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Whitespace Invisibility
description: Whitespace invisibility is the kayo pattern where trailing spaces, non-breaking spaces, and zero-width characters make 'Smith' and 'Smith ' different keys that look identical. The resolution rule is to normalize (strip, collapse, remove zero-width code points) at ingest and to visualize whitespace in admin tools. Copy-paste from web pages and PDFs is the usual vector.
demo:
s = 'Smith\u200b '
import re
clean = re.sub(r'[\u200b\u200c\u200d\ufeff]', '', s).strip()
print(repr(s), '->', repr(clean))
print('rule: normalize at ingest; visualize whitespace in admin tools')
provenance: Public reference: standard data-quality and record-linkage literature; verified 2026-10-21.
